summary: GRAS (Generally Recognized As Safe) lets a substance be added to food without FDA premarket approval if qualified experts agree it is safe; for decades a company could self-affirm GRAS and never tell FDA. FDA has signaled it will close that self-affirmation path and is re-reviewing older additives.
impacts: Any ingredient a beverage relies on under self-affirmed GRAS may need a notification or removal; preservatives such as BHA and BHT are early re-review targets.
implications: A beverage maker can no longer assume a self-affirmed ingredient is settled; the industry must hold audit-ready safety files for every additive in use.
action: Inventory every self-affirmed GRAS ingredient in the portfolio and assemble its safety file now; flag any on FDA's re-review list for a reformulation contingency.
cfr: 21 CFR 170.30 (GRAS criteria);21 CFR 170 Subpart E (GRAS notification)

summary: Certified color additives are the synthetic FD&C dyes (Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2, Green 3) listed and batch-certified by FDA. In 2025 FDA and HHS announced a push to phase out petroleum-based dyes, and FDA had already revoked the authorization for FD&C Red No. 3 in food in January 2025.
impacts: Flavored and colored sparkling drinks using certified dyes face reformulation to exempt-from-certification colors; Red No. 3 is a hard removal item.
implications: A color change is also a claims event for the industry: it can support or undercut a 'no artificial colors' statement, so color sourcing becomes a marketing decision, not just an R&D one.
action: Map every SKU's color source; for any certified dye, plan a Part 73 alternative and coordinate the label and claims change.
cfr: 21 CFR Part 74 (certified color additives);21 CFR Part 73 (colors exempt from certification)

summary: There is no legal definition of 'ultra-processed food' yet; FDA and USDA announced they are jointly developing one. Once it exists it becomes a lever for warnings, school restrictions, and marketing pressure.
impacts: Sweetened and heavily formulated beverages, especially those using non-nutritive sweeteners, are likely to land inside whatever definition emerges.
implications: The industry faces a medium-term repositioning question; a definition could reshape claims, school access, and consumer perception across the category.
action: Track the joint FDA and USDA definition work and pressure-test the portfolio against the leading candidate definitions.

summary: FDA proposed a front-of-package nutrition label (a 'Nutrition Info' box) rating Saturated Fat, Sodium, and Added Sugars as Low, Medium, or High on the front panel, amending 21 CFR Part 101.
impacts: For a sweetened drink, added sugar is the most likely 'High' trigger and would reshape the front panel; a zero-sugar line is comparatively well positioned.
implications: Front-of-package ratings could shift category-wide purchasing toward lower-sugar options and make added sugar a visible point-of-sale signal.
action: Model each SKU against the proposed thresholds and sequence any front-panel redesign to absorb the box in one change.

summary: FDA's updated 'healthy' claim rule (21 CFR 101.65) requires a food to fit a food-group model, not just hit nutrient thresholds. It was effective in 2025 with a compliance date of February 25, 2028.
impacts: Any beverage that carries or implies 'healthy' must be re-checked against the new definition before the compliance date; adding vitamins to an unhealthy base no longer qualifies.
implications: The industry loses a long-used marketing lever and must substantiate wellness positioning against a stricter federal standard.
action: Audit every product that uses or implies 'healthy' and remove or substantiate the claim before 2028.

summary: Caffeine added to cola-type beverages is GRAS up to 0.02 percent under 21 CFR 182.1180. FDA is working on voluntary caffeine-labeling guidance for the energy and functional categories and has warned about concentrated caffeine.
impacts: A caffeinated line must keep added caffeine within the GRAS basis for its category and be ready for voluntary labeling expectations.
implications: Energy and functional positioning carries added labeling and safety scrutiny, and intersects Canada's stricter supplemented-foods regime.
action: Confirm per-serving caffeine against the GRAS basis and prepare cautionary-statement copy for markets that expect it.

summary: California AB 418, the California Food Safety Act, bans the manufacture or sale in California of foods containing brominated vegetable oil, potassium bromate, propylparaben, or FD&C Red No. 3, effective January 1, 2027. It parallels FDA's federal revocations of BVO (2024) and Red No. 3 (2025).
impacts: Any California-sold formula containing BVO or Red No. 3 must be reformulated before January 1, 2027; given the federal revocations these are national removal items.
implications: California sets the template other states copy, so its bans effectively become the national floor for the industry.
action: Confirm with R&D and suppliers that no California-sold formula contains the four banned substances and treat BVO and Red No. 3 as national removals.
cfr: Federal parallel: BVO authorization revoked (former 21 CFR 180.30);Federal parallel: FD&C Red No. 3 (21 CFR Part 74)

summary: California AB 660 standardizes date labels: a date, if used, must use the 'BEST if Used By' or 'USE by' family of terms, with 'sell by' banned, effective July 1, 2026.
impacts: Packaging copy on California-sold products must conform by July 1, 2026; this is a label-copy change, not a formula change.
implications: Date-label standardization is spreading and reduces the flexibility brands have in package wording.
action: Update date-label copy for California SKUs before July 1, 2026.

summary: California AB 2316 bans six synthetic dyes from foods sold through school channels, effective December 31, 2027.
impacts: Only products that reach the school channel are affected; core retail lines are not directly covered.
implications: School channels are becoming a distinct, stricter market that the industry must formulate for separately.
action: Confirm whether any SKU reaches school channels and review its colors.

summary: California AB 1264 is an enacted school-focused ultra-processed-food law; CDPH must define terms by June 1, 2028, and the definition names non-nutritive sweeteners such as sucralose.
impacts: Sucralose-sweetened drinks in the school channel may be restricted once the definition is set.
implications: California's UPF definition will likely become a reference other states and channels adopt.
action: Track the CDPH definition and assess school-channel exposure for non-nutritive-sweetened SKUs.

summary: California AB 2244, introduced February 2026, proposes a voluntary 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' seal with retailer good-faith identification, using a UPF definition tied to prior California law.
impacts: Certification could be a shelf differentiator at large retailers; non-certified products may face a perception gap.
implications: A voluntary seal can still pressure the whole category to reformulate to qualify.
action: Decide whether to pursue certification if the bill advances.

summary: Proposition 65 is California's 1986 right-to-know law: it requires a warning when a product exposes a person to one of roughly 1,000 listed chemicals above a safe-harbor level. For beverages the drivers are trace heavy metals and acrylamide.
impacts: Trace heavy metals carried in by botanicals, colors, concentrates, or water can trigger a warning obligation or a bounty-driven lawsuit; bottled water and botanical drinks carry the most exposure.
implications: Exposure, not harm, triggers enforcement, so the industry carries ongoing testing and supplier-indemnity cost regardless of actual risk.
action: Maintain annual heavy-metal and acrylamide testing for California-sold products, secure supplier attestation and indemnity, and warn where a safe-harbor level cannot be met.

summary: More than 140 ingredient bills across 42 states (13 enacted) target over 100 ingredients, with California setting the template.
impacts: A nationally distributed product generally must meet the strictest state's rule or maintain separate formulations.
implications: The patchwork is the central cost driver, pushing the industry toward function-tagged ingredient management and proactive reformulation.
action: Maintain the function-tagged ingredient master list and promote confirmed bills into per-state rows.

summary: Iowa enacted a school-food ingredient law naming synthetic dyes and other additives.
impacts: Affects products sold through Iowa school channels only.
implications: Part of the multistate school-food wave that fragments the school market.
action: Confirm school-channel exposure and the colors used.

summary: Nebraska enacted a school-food ingredient law naming synthetic dyes and other additives.
impacts: Affects products sold through Nebraska school channels only.
implications: Part of the multistate school-food wave that fragments the school market.
action: Confirm school-channel exposure and the colors used.

summary: Tennessee enacted a school-food ingredient law naming synthetic dyes and other additives.
impacts: Affects products sold through Tennessee school channels only.
implications: Part of the multistate school-food wave that fragments the school market.
action: Confirm school-channel exposure and the colors used.

summary: A California bill would create a state-level GRAS review process, part of the broader state GRAS-reporting trend.
impacts: Adds a state reporting and review burden on additives used in California-sold products.
implications: A state-by-state GRAS patchwork would multiply compliance cost across the industry.
action: Monitor the bill and inventory self-affirmed GRAS additives in use.

summary: New Jersey is debating a state GRAS reporting bill.
impacts: Potential state reporting burden on additives used in New Jersey-sold products.
implications: Adds to the state GRAS-reporting trend and the cost of a patchwork.
action: Monitor the bill and inventory self-affirmed GRAS additives.

summary: New York is debating a state GRAS reporting bill.
impacts: Potential state reporting burden on additives used in New York-sold products.
implications: Adds to the state GRAS-reporting trend and the cost of a patchwork.
action: Monitor the bill and inventory self-affirmed GRAS additives.

summary: New Jersey filed one of the first state ingredient bills in 2023.
impacts: Could restrict named additives in New Jersey-sold products if advanced.
implications: An early signal that the ingredient patchwork reaches beyond California.
action: Confirm the bill's current status against state text.

summary: West Virginia enacted a statewide ingredient ban, subject to litigation.
impacts: Could block sale of affected SKUs in West Virginia once effective.
implications: States can ban outright, so the strictest state effectively sets the national floor.
action: Confirm effective dates and the affected ingredients against state text.

summary: Texas label-warning legislation has been slowed by litigation but keeps recurring.
impacts: Could require warning text on labels of Texas-sold products if enacted.
implications: Signals that label-warning policy is spreading beyond California.
action: Monitor the litigation and any refiling.

summary: Twenty-three states approved SNAP waivers restricting sweetened or carbonated beverages, with effective dates rolling out 2026 to 2028.
impacts: Sweetened and possibly broadly worded zero-sugar sparkling lines may be SNAP-ineligible in some states.
implications: Point-of-sale eligibility now varies by state, affecting volume in SNAP-heavy channels.
action: Do a state-by-state read of which products are caught by the actual waiver wording.

summary: Health Canada's Supplemented Foods Regulations govern foods with added supplemental ingredients (including caffeine and certain vitamins), requiring a Supplemented Food Facts table, cautionary statements, and caffeine limits.
impacts: A caffeinated or functional beverage sold in Canada may need cautionary statements and must stay within Canadian caffeine limits, which can differ from the US basis.
implications: Canada is a stricter functional-beverage market, so US formulations and labels may not port directly across the border.
action: Map any Canada-distributed SKU to the supplemented-foods requirements: caffeine limit, cautionary statements, and the Supplemented Food Facts table.

summary: Mexico's NOM-051 front-of-pack labeling requires black octagon warning seals for products high in calories, sugars, saturated fat, or sodium, plus disclaimer legends when a product contains non-nutritive sweeteners or added caffeine.
impacts: A sweetened or non-nutritive-sweetened beverage sold in Mexico likely carries one or more octagon seals and a sweetener disclaimer, and faces marketing-to-children restrictions.
implications: Mexico is the strictest front-of-pack regime the portfolio meets and a preview of where warning-label policy can go.
action: For Mexico-distributed SKUs, determine the octagon seals and sweetener or caffeine legends triggered and confirm packaging compliance.
